title: DNS and the Gateway API
summary: Names inside the cluster, and one front door for HTTP from outside.

steps.title: Cluster DNS
body: CoreDNS gives every Service a name:
A pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` has search domains for its own namespace, so from a pod in `shop`:
payments.shop.svc.cluster.local  the full name, always works
payments (from a pod in 'blog')  fails: looks for payments.blog...
Debug DNS from inside the cluster, not your laptop:

steps.prompt: A pod in namespace `blog` must call Service `auth` in namespace `identity`. Which URL works?
steps.explain: Short names only resolve in your own namespace. Add `.identity` (or use the full name).

steps.title: Call a Service in another namespace
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `cart` (namespace `shop`) calls the `payments` Service, which lives in the namespace `payments`. Its log
says it cannot: `kubectl -n shop logs deploy/cart --tail=3`.
1. Write the **fully qualified** DNS name of the `payments` Service into `~/answers/fqdn.txt`.
2. Fix `cart`'s `PAYMENTS_URL` (an environment variable on the Deployment) so that it reaches payments; its newest log

checks.name: fqdn.txt is the Service's full name
checks.fail: Not the full name. A Service is `NAME.NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local`.

checks.name: cart reaches payments
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop rollout status deploy/cart --timeout=30s >/dev/null && sleep 4 && kubectl -n shop logs $(kubectl -n shop get pods -l app=cart -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .metadata.name') --tail=1
checks.fail: `cart`'s newest log line does not say `payments OK`. A short name only resolves in the pod's own namespace.

hints: `kubectl -n shop exec deploy/cart -- cat /etc/resolv.conf` shows the search list: `shop.svc.cluster.local` comes first.
`payments` alone means `payments.shop...`; add the namespace: `payments.payments`, or the full name.
solution: kubectl -n shop exec deploy/cart -- nslookup payments.payments.svc.cluster.local
steps.explain: Pods resolve names through CoreDNS with a search list that starts with their own namespace, so `payments` from `shop` looks for `payments.shop.svc.cluster.local`. Across namespaces use `NAME.NAMESPACE` or the full name. With `ndots:5`, external names get the search list tried first, which is why the trailing dot (`api.example.com.`) is a known latency trick.

steps.title: Gateway API: one front door
body: One LoadBalancer per app gets expensive and gives you no HTTP routing. The **Gateway API** splits the front door into two objects, owned by two teams:
- a **Gateway** (platform team): the listener, its port, hostname and TLS certificate, and which controller runs it (`gatewayClassName`);
- **HTTPRoutes** (app teams, in their own namespace): "this host and path go to this Service".
A **Gateway controller** (Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, Traefik, NGINX Gateway Fabric, or the cloud's own) runs the proxy pods that actually receive traffic and apply the routes.
- name: public            # the Gateway to attach to
- name: shop-api         # a Service in this namespace
A Gateway with **no controller installed does nothing**: it never gets an address. TLS terminates at the Gateway, using the certificate Secret its listener names.

> **Note:** You will still meet the older **Ingress** object (`kind: Ingress`, `ingressClassName`, `pathType: Prefix`) in existing clusters. The Ingress API is frozen and the popular ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026, so new setups use the Gateway API. The routing ideas are the same.

steps.prompt: Complete the HTTPRoute that sends `api.shop.example.com/orders` and everything under it to Service `orders` on port 8080.
steps.explain: `hostnames` is a list, `PathPrefix` matches `/orders` and `/orders/...` (`Exact` would match only `/orders`), and `backendRefs` names the Service and its port.

steps.prompt: You applied a Gateway and an HTTPRoute, but every request times out. `kubectl get gateway public -n gateway` shows an empty `ADDRESS` column and `PROGRAMMED` is `False` (or `Unknown`). Most likely?
options: No Gateway controller is installed (or `gatewayClassName` names a GatewayClass that does not exist)
The Service type must be LoadBalancer
steps.explain: The controller fills in the ADDRESS and sets `Programmed: True` once it has set up the proxy for the Gateway. Check `kubectl get gatewayclass` (its `ACCEPTED` should be `True`) and the controller's pods. A missing `hostnames` would only make the route match every host.

steps.prompt: A `PathPrefix` match compares whole path segments, and the longest matching prefix wins. One HTTPRoute for `shop.example.com` has these three rules. Which backend handles `/api/orders/7`? Type the Service name.
steps.explain: `/api/admin` does not match. Of `/` and `/api`, the longer one wins. Note `/apiary` would *not* match `/api`: Prefix compares segments, not characters.

steps.title: Route traffic with a Gateway API HTTPRoute
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). It has the **Gateway API** CRDs (v1.7) installed, and the platform team's Gateway `public` in the
namespace `shop` (`kubectl get gateway -n shop`). There is no gateway controller in this small cluster, so nothing
serves traffic, but the API server validates your route exactly as a real cluster would.
Write and apply an `HTTPRoute` named `shop` in the namespace `shop`, attached to the Gateway `public`, for the host
1. requests whose path starts with `/api` go to the Service `api` on port 80;
2. everything else goes to the Service `web` on port 80.

checks.name: the HTTPRoute shop exists and is attached to the Gateway public
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop get httproute shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.parentRefs[0].name} {.spec.hostnames}'
checks.fail: There is no HTTPRoute `shop` in `shop` attached to `public` for `shop.example.com`.

checks.name: /api goes to the api Service, everything else to web
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop get httproute shop -o json | jq -r '.spec.rules[] | "\(.matches[0].path.type // "-") \(.matches[0].path.value // "-") -> \(.backendRefs[0].name):\(.backendRefs[0].port)"' | sort
checks.fail: The rules should send `PathPrefix /api` to `api:80` and `PathPrefix /` to `web:80`.

hints: `spec.hostnames: [shop.example.com]`; each rule has `matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}}]` and `backendRefs: [{name: api, port: 80}]`.
The longest matching prefix wins, so the `/` rule can sit next to the `/api` one.
solution: kubectl -n shop get httproute shop -o yaml
steps.explain: The Gateway API splits what Ingress mixed together: the platform team owns the `Gateway` (listeners, TLS, which controller), application teams own `HTTPRoute`s that attach to it. Since ingress-nginx was retired in March 2026, this is the API new clusters use; Ingress objects still exist in many clusters and translate almost one to one (`ingress2gateway` does it). On a real cluster, `kubectl get httproute shop -o yaml` would also show `status.parents[].conditions` with `Accepted` and `ResolvedRefs`.
